options: Every resource Terraform manages, along with the last-known attributes it set on each one
A copy of the HCL configuration files, nothing else
Only the provider version constraints
A history of every terraform command ever run
questions.explain: State is Terraform's record of exactly what it created and its last-known real-world attributes -- its only memory of what it manages.

questions.q: Why does terraform plan need the state file?
options: To compare the desired configuration against what Terraform last knew existed, so it can decide create vs. update vs. leave alone
State is not actually used during terraform plan
To store the Azure subscription credentials
To generate the provider plugin code
questions.explain: Without a baseline to diff against, every plan would look like creating everything from scratch, even for resources that already exist.

questions.q: What happens if terraform.tfstate is deleted?
options: Terraform "forgets" the resources it manages, and the next plan proposes creating duplicates of resources that already exist in Azure
Nothing changes -- Terraform rebuilds state automatically from the HCL files alone
All real Azure resources are immediately deleted
Terraform refuses to run any command ever again
questions.explain: State is the only link between the HCL and the real resources; losing it makes Terraform think nothing has been created yet.

questions.q: Why is hand-editing the state file risky?
options: Terraform never validates a manual edit, so you can desynchronize its understanding of reality without it knowing anything is wrong
Terraform automatically rejects any file with unexpected formatting
It is actually the officially recommended way to fix drift
State files cannot be opened as plain text
questions.explain: A manual edit bypasses any of Terraform's own checks, so the next apply can act on information that no longer matches reality.

questions.q: Why does this lesson defer the fix for local state's team hazard to Lesson 17?
options: Because storing state remotely with locking is a separate topic -- "State Management & Remote State" -- covered properly later
Because remote state is never actually necessary for real teams
Because Lesson 17 replaces Terraform with Bicep entirely
Because local state has no real downsides worth discussing further
questions.explain: This lesson establishes why local state is risky for teams; Lesson 17 is where the remote-backend solution is actually configured.
